59645eb3208ce069: KUALA LUMPUR: KLIA Ekspres services were disrupted this morning following a cable cut between Putrajaya and Cyberjaya and Salak Tinggi stations.
In a statement of Facebook, the operator said the combined train service would remain in effect until further notice.
Since 5am, trains have been operating every 20 minutes from both KL Sentral and KLIA Terminal 2, stopping at all stations.
The operator said its technical team was working to rectify the issue and restore normal train services as soon as possible.
Passengers have been advised to check with station personnel for the latest updates and assistance.
The operator apologised for the inconvenience and thanked passengers for their patience and understanding.
NST has contacted the authorities for comment on the incident.
a51299badf6f60e6: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 12 — Malaysia has begun the recall process for the pre-facelift (FL) version of Omoda 5. While this is the 2nd major recall announcement for the SUV (the 1st recall happened in 2024), the reason is the same: Omoda 5’s rear axle.

The recall announcement was published on Chery Malaysia’s social media platforms several hours after the Road Transport Department (JPJ) said that it has temporarily suspended Vehicle Type Approval (VTA) for the Omoda 5 following a recent incident in Johor where the SUV’s rear axle detached while on the move.

JPJ also said that it has instructed Chery to identify and recall all units that are potentially at risk. Meanwhile, Chery said that all affected vehicles will receive comprehensive inspections, and any required follow-up actions, including component replacements, will be free of charge.

Omoda 5 was originally launched in July 2023 but has since been replaced by a facelifted model called Chery 05 last September. Chery 05 is equipped with a multi-link rear suspension system as opposed to the torsion beam setup on the Omoda 5.
Similarly, the fully electric Omoda E5 also comes with multi-link suspension on its rear. All three Chery models are locally assembled (CKD) at Inokom’s plant in Kulim, Kedah.

912b6e15ec33d6af: BEIJING, Oct 12 — Zheng Qinwen became the first home winner of the China Open yesterday as she beat Russian teenager Mirra Andreeva 7-5, 6-4 in the final.
The former world number four and reigning Olympic champion was a wildcard entry in Beijing, having struggled with form and fitness after elbow surgery in 2025.
It was the 54th-ranked Zheng’s first title in nearly two years, and tears filled her eyes as she fell to the court in celebration.
“The feeling was incredible to win here in Beijing... in front of my home crowd is one of my dreams,” she said during the trophy ceremony.
“I’ve been through a very, very tough year,” she added.
She congratulated Andreeva on her French Open win from earlier this year before serenading the crowd with a song about chasing the “light of dreams”.
Zheng, 24, is the first Chinese player to win the prestigious tournament since its inception in 2004.
Andreeva, ranked fifth, was more consistent to start with, but Zheng grabbed back a break and stayed with her 19-year-old opponent as they battled on the baseline.
Zheng saved three set points to level at 5-5 and won every single point after that, sending down an ace to take the first set.
A crowd desperate to see their homegrown talent crowned champion was at times disruptive as cheers erupted before points ended and shouts for Zheng punctuated serves on both sides of the net.
But the players kept their focus, holding serve until Zheng found a way through in the ninth game of the second set, firing brilliantly against the line to break and go up 5-4.
A double-fault threatened to derail an imminent triumph until Zheng, defiant, sent down an ace to win on her first match point.
‘Want to give everything’
It is Zheng’s first trophy since October 2024 when she beat Sofia Kenin in Tokyo, and her first-ever title at the WTA 1000 level.
Ending the title drought was not easy.
“I felt like I just forgot how to compete after coming back from injury,” she told reporters.
Concerns with her elbow forced her to retire from last year’s China Open in the third round, which preceded a string of disappointing results.
“Finally, after so many losses, I (found) my fire again,” she said.
The finalists’ only previous meeting was in the 2024 China Open quarter-finals, where Zheng beat Andreeva in three sets.
Andreeva, playing in her first China Open final, said it was “a very nice week” despite falling just short.
With her run, Andreeva is set to move up to a career-high ranking of third.
Both players are scheduled to compete this week at the 1000-level tournament in Wuhan, with Zheng facing American Ann Li in the first round and Andreeva starting in the second.
“I’m so hungry, honestly, for what’s gonna come next,” Zheng added yesterday. “I just want to give everything.” — AFP
f4a6c2512840af64: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 12 — Government measures to address the gap in access to doctors, specialists and diagnostic facilities between urban hospitals and rural healthcare facilities will be among the key focuses of today’s Dewan Rakyat session.

According to the Order of Business on the Parliament’s website, the issue will be raised by Datuk Seri Jalaluddin Alias (BN-Jelebu), who will ask the Health Minister to explain the government’s measures to address the disparity during the question-and-answer session.

Also in focus is a question from Muhammad Fawwaz Mohamad Jan (PN-Permatang Pauh) to the Investment, Trade and Industry Minister on the risks of the country’s export dependence on the electrical and electronics (E&E) sector, which accounts for nearly half of total exports, as well as diversification strategies should the global semiconductor cycle weaken.

Mohd Isam Mohd Isa (BN-Tampin) will ask the Rural and Regional Development Minister to explain the strategic justification for the establishment of the first MARA hospital, including the status of studies and planning, its location, bed capacity, areas of specialisation, estimated development cost, funding sources and expected commencement of operations.

In the same session, Rushdan Rusmi (PN-Padang Besar) will ask the Home Minister to detail the government’s integrated measures to combat people smuggling, drugs and prohibited goods through unofficial routes along the Perlis border, including action against the syndicate networks involved.

Also listed is a question from Jimmy Puah Wee Tse (PH-Tebrau) on the government’s long-term policies to address climate change and the implementation timeline for the postponed carbon tax to ensure Malaysia’s competitiveness in a low-carbon economy.

Kamal Ashaari (PN-Kuala Krau) will ask the Entrepreneur and Cooperatives Development Minister to explain the monitoring measures and interventions in place to ensure that Koperasi Permodalan Felda Malaysia Berhad (KPF) settles outstanding share redemption payments owed to more than 9,000 members, including the setting of a payment timeline.

This week’s Dewan Rakyat sitting will also see the start of the policy-stage debate on the Supply Bill 2027, following the tabling of Budget 2027 by Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim, who is also Finance Minister, on Friday.

According to the Dewan Rakyat calendar for the Third Meeting of the Fifth Session of the 15th Parliament, the policy-stage debate on Budget 2027 will run from Oct 12 to 22, followed by a four-day winding-up session by relevant ministers beginning Oct 26.
The Dewan Rakyat sitting will run for 37 days until Dec 8. — Bernama
b2c0b819daaae6a9: LIVERPOOL, Oct 12 — Manchester City shrugged off the threat of swingeing sanctions to beat 10-man Liverpool 3-0 in their first game since being found guilty on more than 100 charges of breaking Premier League financial rules.
Second-half goals from Erling Haaland, Jeremy Doku and Rayan Cherki extended City’s flawless start under Enzo Maresca after Ryan Gravenberch had been sent off for two yellow cards.
City re-established their three-point lead at the top of the table, but the future of any title challenge rests on the outcome of the club’s appeal against widespread financial impropriety.
“We need to learn how to deal with the outside noise, but make our own noise, which is to win games,” said Maresca.
“Our fans were singing at the end, so the noise was from us.”
An independent commission found City and their Emirati owners arranged “sham” deals to artificially inflate revenues and reduce costs by more than £900 million (US$1.2 billion) between 2009 and 2018.
No sanction has yet been handed down, but a severe points deduction or even expulsion from the English top flight are on the table unless City overturn the decision.
There has even been speculation there could be retrospective action to strip titles.
“The uncertainty is not good for anyone,” said Liverpool boss Andoni Iraola.
The multiple breaches of Premier League laws came during a period in which City won three titles and a clutch of other trophies.
City’s rivals believe, however, that the illegal spending during that period also built the foundations for a golden era under former boss Pep Guardiola, who left at the end of last season.
Liverpool were one of the clubs most affected, having finished second to City three times in the past 12 years.
“City have fundamentally cheated to win those leagues,” Jamie Gallaghie, a 48-year-old teacher, told AFP.

The visitors arrived under the protection of a police escort with a hostile Anfield welcome expected, but there was no repeat of the violent scenes when their team bus was pelted by bottles ahead of a Champions League clash in 2018.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Manchester City striker Erling Haaland celebrates with teammate Matheus Nunes after scoring the opening goal against Liverpool during their English Premier League match at Anfield in Liverpool, England, on October 11, 2026. — AFP pic
‘A generation of supporters cheated’

Liverpool fans lined the streets to greet the City players with chants of “cheats” and “going down”, while merchandise stalls were littered with flags and scarves mocking their rivals’ financial scandal.
In the iconic Kop end behind one goal a banner read “a generation of supporters cheated.”
The battles between Guardiola’s City and Jurgen Klopp’s Liverpool in recent years became the Premier League’s marquee event.
But with the eyes of the world watching, Liverpool failed to rise to the occasion on the field.
New Liverpool boss Iraola’s options were blunted without the injured Dominik Szoboszlai, Alexander Isak and Cody Gakpo as the Spaniard suffered his first defeat since taking charge of the Reds.
An Abu Dhabi-backed takeover in 2008 transformed City from mid-table mediocrity into the dominant force of the English game.
City’s economic might was on full show and helped turn the game as Maresca could introduce Doku off the bench early in the second half.
Within minutes the Belgian winger had been chopped down by Gravenberch, who was shown a harsh second booking, and Liverpool never recovered.
Doku’s deflected shot was then smashed home by Haaland to break the deadlock 25 minutes from time, opening the floodgates.
Three minutes later Doku curled a sensational strike into the top corner himself.
Cherki then exchanged a slick one-two with Josko Gvardiol before slotting under Alisson Becker to rub salt in Liverpool wounds.
The defeat leaves Liverpool nine points adrift of the leaders down in ninth. — AFP
e45207aa1a996a3b: DUNGUN: Former Bukit Besi assemblyman Roslee Daud died early this morning. He was 66.
Roslee, who suffered from heart complications, died at Dungun Hospital at 5.30am.
He served as Umno and Barisan Nasional's Bukit Besi assemblyman for two terms from May 2013 to August 2023.
Roslee also served as a Terengganu executive council member in charge of rural development, entrepreneurs, cooperatives and consumers.
Funeral prayers will be held at Masjid Bukit Besi after Zohor prayers, followed by burial at the Bukit Besi Islamic Cemetery.
5f8af39627472d6d: HONG KONG, Oct 12 — The ashes of late Hong Kong Cantopop singer Anita Mui have reportedly been stolen from a columbarium at Hong Kong’s Po Lin Monastery, with no arrests made nearly three months after the disappearance.

According to Hong Kong media outlet The Standard, the incident was discovered on July 18 when a fan visiting the monastery to pay respects noticed that the screws on the door of the compartment containing Anita’s urn were loose and the urn was missing.
The fan subsequently alerted Anita’s family and reported the matter to the police.

With no significant progress in the investigation, Anita’s family and fan club made a joint appeal for public information on Saturday (Oct 10), the day that would have marked the singer’s 63rd birthday.
Sources cited by The Standard said no ransom demand had been made, and no other urns at the columbarium were reported missing.

During a livestream early on Sunday, Poon Siu-man, a close friend of Anita’s mother, explained that the family and fan club had decided to disclose the incident in hopes of drawing greater media and public attention.

The announcement was made after longtime fans gathered for their annual commemoration of Anita’s birthday, with the family hoping that public assistance could help identify those responsible and recover the urn.
Another fan club, Mui Nation, described the incident as “extremely absurd and contrary to ethics and morality,” The Standard reported.
The club called for a thorough police investigation and urged the columbarium’s management to review potential security lapses and account for any shortcomings. — AsiaOne
b17a4f95d8966bd1: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 12 — The ringgit opened higher against the US dollar today, supported by the government’s commitment to fiscal discipline following the tabling of Budget 2027 last Friday.
At 8am, the ringgit edged up to 4.0820/0880 against the greenback from Friday’s close of 4.0830/0875.

Bank Muamalat Malaysia Bhd chief economist Dr Mohd Afzanizam Abdul Rashid said the government’s commitment to fiscal discipline was reflected in its target to narrow the fiscal deficit to 3.3 per cent of gross domestic product in 2027, from an estimated 3.6 per cent this year.
He said the pragmatic approach should help preserve Malaysia’s sovereign credit rating, providing firm support for the ringgit.
However, he said external conditions remained uncertain, particularly developments in West Asia and their potential impact on global crude oil prices.
“Hence, attention will be on whether the US Federal Reserve will consider raising interest rates further this month.
“Therefore, we expect the ringgit-US dollar pair to maintain its tight-range bias today,” he told Bernama.
At the opening, the ringgit traded mostly higher against a basket of major and ASEAN currencies.

The local note strengthened against the British pound to 5.4038/4117 from 5.4063/4123 at Friday’s close and rose against the euro to 4.5735/5802 from 4.5807/5858 previously. However, it weakened against the Japanese yen to 2.5806/5846 from 2.5791/5821 on Friday.
Against ASEAN currencies, the ringgit edged up against the Singapore dollar to 3.1876/1928 from 3.1896/1934 at Friday’s close and the Thai baht to 12.1720/1957 from 12.1735/1909 previously.
The local note also ticked up against the Indonesian rupiah to 228.0/228.4 from 228.1/228.4 at Friday’s close, while remaining unchanged against the Philippine peso at 6.50/6.51. — Bernama
be6850f6366083c3: KUALA LUMPUR: Merz Aesthetics is strengthening its focus on Malaysia and the wider Asia-Pacific medical aesthetics market as the industry shifts towards skin longevity, personalised treatments and research-driven innovation.

The global medical aesthetics company has launched a regional campaign featuring Hollywood actress Lucy Liu as its ambassador while planning a research and development innovation centre in Singapore to advance research into skin ageing and longevity.

The initiatives reflect the industry's drive to move beyond conventional anti-ageing treatments toward more comprehensive, science-backed approaches that support long-term skin health and natural-looking results.

Asia-Pacific is emerging as a key growth market for medical aesthetics, supported by rising consumer acceptance of non-surgical procedures, growing awareness of aesthetic treatments and demand for more personalised care.

Industry research by MarketsandMarkets projects the regional medical aesthetics market to grow from US$3.75 billion in 2025 to US$8.66 billion by 2031, driven partly by demand for injectables and minimally invasive treatments.

In Malaysia, the aesthetic medicine market has also expanded alongside greater consumer interest in self-care and appearance-related treatments. Market estimates cited in a 2026 industry study put the sector's revenue at RM818.3 million in 2024, up from RM550.1 million in 2022.

As competition intensifies, providers and manufacturers are increasingly focusing on clinical evidence, practitioner expertise and treatment outcomes, while consumers place greater emphasis on safety, credibility and natural-looking results. These trends are also raising the importance of medical training and appropriate clinical oversight as the industry expands.

Unveiled in Seoul, South Korea, the campaign positions skin longevity and personalised aesthetic treatments as key growth areas, responding to changing consumer expectations among women across the Asia-Pacific.

Merz Aesthetics chief scientific officer Samantha Kerr said advances in the understanding of skin longevity were reshaping the medical aesthetics industry, with scientific research playing an increasingly important role in treatment development.

Alongside the campaign launch, Merz Aesthetics announced plans to establish a new Research & Development Innovation Center in Singapore, strengthening its commitment to skin science and its global research and development network.

The planned centre is expected to advance the company's research into skin ageing and longevity. However, details on the investment value, development timeline and operational scope have not been disclosed.
a75d6548e35e43ff: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 12 — Two local men arrested following a police chase along Jalan Wangsa 5, Bukit Antarabangsa heading towards the Middle Ring Road 2 (MRR2) in Hulu Kelang here yesterday, were found to be in possession of sharp weapons, cable-theft equipment, and drugs inside their vehicle.

Ampang Jaya District Police Chief ACP Khairul Anuar Khalid said both suspects were apprehended when their Isuzu Dmax vehicle was intercepted at the junction of Jalan Jelatek and Jalan Taman Setiawangsa near the Caltex station in Setiawangsa.

“An inspection of the suspects’ vehicle led to the discovery of dangerous weapons such as a machete (parang) and a sickle, as well as cable-theft tools like a manhole opener. Also seized were substances suspected to be drugs,” he said in a statement yesterday.

He added that the case is being investigated under Section 186 of the Penal Code for obstructing a public servant in the discharge of public functions, and Section 6(1) of the Corrosive and Explosive Substances and Offensive Weapons Act 1958 for carrying or possessing offensive weapons in public places.

Investigations are also being conducted under Section 29(1) of minor offences Act 1955 for possessing or conveying property suspected of being stolen or fraudulently obtained, and Section 12(2) of the Dangerous Drugs Act 1952 for drug possession.
Yesterday, several videos went viral on social media showing members of the public assisting police in chasing the two suspects, who attempted to flee after colliding with public vehicles. — Bernama
26057848d52f56af: BANGKOK: British finance minister John Healey will stress the importance of budget discipline and improving resilience to geopolitical shocks when he meets his foreign counterparts on his first trip to the International Monetary Fund's annual meetings this week.

"I will work with our international partners to keep trade moving, support families and businesses, and make Britain's economy stronger and more resilient," Healey said in a statement released by his office.

Healey will argue that major economies need credible plans to get borrowing under control, the finance ministry said, following similar calls last week from IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva and Bank of England Governor Andrew Bailey.

* The IMF and World Bank hold their annual meetings this week in Bangkok, where finance ministers and central bank chiefs will discuss the impact of the widening war in the Middle East and its effect on energy prices and inflation.
* Healey will meet Ukrainian Finance Minister Sergii Marchenko, among others, to discuss resilience.

* Last week major economies' government borrowing costs hit their highest in decades, driven by investor worries about inflation caused by the US-Iran war, high levels of government borrowing and the need for higher interest rates.

* Healey repeated that he would deliver "fiscal discipline" at his first annual budget on October 28, when he will need to take steps to keep plans to lower borrowing on track in the face of higher debt interest costs and a desire to spend more on defence and reduce energy costs.

* Britain's Institute for Fiscal Studies estimates Healey will need £36 billion of tax rises – equivalent to raising the main rate of income tax by 3.0 percentage points – if he wants to fully offset the erosion of government budgets caused by higher inflation and fund extra defence spending
2cf5bac18f1e7c47: RIYADH, Oct 12 — A fresh Houthi strike hit Riyadh’s international airport yesterday, a day after an attack claimed by the Yemeni group killed at least a dozen people and forced authorities to suspend operations there.

Saturday’s attack, the deadliest on Saudi soil in more than a decade, was a sharp escalation in the Yemen war, where Riyadh has long militarily supported the internationally recognised government against the Houthis.

The Iran-backed group yesterday claimed multiple attacks over the last 24 hours, including on the airport, and threatened to keep targeting the kingdom’s transit hubs, calling them “a theatre of operations for our forces”.
Hours later, the Saudi-led coalition fighting the group reported that a projectile struck King Khalid International Airport, sparking a fire. Air defences also intercepted a missile nearby, it added.
The fresh attack on the airport killed one person — a Pakistani resident — and wounded 11 others, Saudi Arabia’s civil aviation authority said.
The wounded “were immediately transferred to several hospitals to receive the necessary medical care,” the authority said on X.
“The attack also caused property damage, the extent of which is currently being assessed.”
Authorities have extended the closure of the airport by 24 hours until 2100 GMT today, the tracking site Flightradar24 said on X.
AFP journalists and locals reported hearing the sound of multiple blasts in the Saudi capital yesterday.
“The birds went into a frenzy after the sound. The whole house shook,” said one resident of the Al-Aarid neighbourhood in the north of the city.

The civil aviation authority also reported another attack on Dammam airport in the east — which the Houthis also said they had targeted — a day after the Saudi coalition reported a projectile landing nearby.
Shortly afterwards, the coalition reported shooting down a drone, also in the east.
‘Full-fledged war crime’
The Houthis have stepped up their attacks on the Riyadh airport — where three people were also killed on Thursday — as well as on Saudi oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.
Although Saudi Arabia has poured billions into its military, Houthi attacks continue to slip through.

“Saudi air defences have been able to intercept some Houthi missile and drone attacks, but Saudi Arabia is so large that it’s simply impossible for them to consistently defend themselves,” said Thomas Juneau, security analyst at Ottawa University.
The anti-Houthi coalition called Saturday’s attack a “full-fledged war crime” and vowed to “respond decisively”.
Houthi media reported two Saudi strikes in Yemen’s Houthi-controlled Sanaa governorate yesterday.
Saturday’s attack drew condemnation from the United Nations and leaders around the world, including US President Donald Trump, who said he was considering joining Saudi strikes against the Houthis.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, whose country does not have diplomatic relations with Saudi Arabia, also denounced the “horrific terrorist attack”.
Four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshis, one American, one Egyptian, one Jordanian, one Syrian, one Palestinian and one Sudanese were killed, the civil aviation authority said, with 309 people wounded.
The Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia also said one of its citizens died yesterday after being wounded the day before.
Operations suspended
An aviation source said airport radar and communications equipment had been damaged and runways needed to be assessed.
Witnesses to Saturday’s strike described chaos in the aftermath.
“People who were in Terminal 3 started running towards us,” a 32-year-old Riyadh resident told AFP.
“Some had lost a hand or an arm. People were running while carrying injured people, covered in blood.”
The attack prompted health officials to activate a rare mass call-up of doctors, a medical source said.

The US, Canadian, German and Spanish embassies in Saudi Arabia have warned their citizens to avoid Riyadh airport, while Australia urged its citizens yesterday to stay indoors altogether and “shelter in place”.
Fighting in Yemen
Saturday’s airport strike, on the eve of Saudi Arabia’s high-profile convention and entertainment season, was the deadliest attack in the kingdom since a 2015 suicide bombing.
With the summer heat subsiding, October also usually marks the beginning of the high travel season for Umrah pilgrims, with millions of Muslims from across the world flocking to Mecca.

Saudi Arabia leads an international coalition that has supported Yemen’s government militarily since 2015, including by seeking to exert control over Yemeni airspace and the airport in the Houthi-held capital Sanaa.
Ottawa University’s Juneau said the Houthis now “want to do to Saudi Arabia what Saudi Arabia does to them”.

On the ground in Yemen, Saudi-supported government forces were advancing in their counter-offensive against the Houthis around the Bab al-Mandab strait, a key shipping route, military sources said Saturday.
The Houthis claimed to have repelled them.
Claims by both sides have been impossible to independently verify, with the situation moving fast on the ground and access for journalists difficult. — AFP
4d5ddf8fd7a51ce4: SELAYANG: Malaysia's 14-year-old footballer Lim You broke down in tears after a 4-0 defeat to India on Sunday, that ended their hopes of qualifying for next year's U-17 Women's Asian Cup.
The youngster, who played the full 90 minutes at the Selayang Stadium, struggled to contain her emotions after the final whistle as Malaysia failed to match India in the Group E decider.
Former Youth and Sports Minister Hannah Yeoh, who was at the stadium to support the national team, approached Lim You to comfort her and offer words of encouragement.
Hannah, now Minister in the Prime Minister's Department (Federal Territories), stayed until the final whistle to support the young Malaysians.
Despite the defeat, Lim You had impressed in earlier matches, showing plenty of promise for the future of women's football in the country.
The United States-based player started the qualifying campaign as a substitute against Syria before coming on for the final 30 minutes and helping Malaysia record a 1-0 victory.
She continued her impressive form against Iraq, helping Malaysia to a 4-0 win and earning the Player of the Match award.
But India proved a different proposition as Takayoshi Ishihara's side struggled to cope with their opponents' dominance.
Lim You started on the right wing before switching to the left after the break.
India took the lead through Redima Devi Chingkhamayum in the 28th minute before Pritika Barman doubled their advantage early in the second half.
Anushka Kumari made it 3-0 three minutes later, while Nidhi Kumar completed the rout in the 86th minute.
Malaysia goalkeeper Putri Aina Husna Mohd Subri produced several fine saves to prevent an even heavier defeat.
The defeat left Malaysia second in Group E with six points from two wins and one defeat, ending their hopes of reaching the finals in China, which will be held from March 3-April 17.
Only group winners qualify for the tournament proper.

6cd43ede1ffddc72: KUALA LUMPUR: A Special Branch policeman who claims he was assaulted by Malaysian Border Control and Protection Agency (MCBA) director-general Datuk Seri Mohd Shuhaily Mohd Zain has lodged another police report to provide new evidence.
Lawyers Kamal Hisham Ja'afar and Muhammad Nor Tamrin said their client, Lance Corporal Mohammad Faiz Muhamad Saman, 40, lodged the report at the Sungai Besi police station on Oct 10.
In the report, Faiz claimed he was taking photographs on his mobile phone of an incident at Kuala Lumpur International Airport (KLIA) Terminal 1 when his device was seized.
He claimed he was then wrongfully detained, assaulted, manhandled and intimidated.
In a statement today, the lawyers said the facts of the case pointed to possible offences under Sections 186, 323, 353, 355 and 506 of the Penal Code.

The provisions cover obstructing a public servant in the discharge of official duties, voluntarily causing hurt, using criminal force to deter a public servant from performing his duties, assault or criminal force with intent to dishonour a person, and criminal intimidation.
The law firm alleged that Faiz and another lance corporal, Muhammad Ekmal Sofwan Driman, who serve as Travel Control Officers (TCO), were assaulted by Shuhaily in a public area.
The lawyers claimed the incident caused injuries and affected their clients' dignity.

The firm also said it was considering legal action against those who made false statements about the lawyers and their clients, including claims that their legal fees were being paid by a criminal syndicate.
Previously, Ekmal and Faiz denied claims that they were acting as touts or involved in "counter setting".

Today, the firm said the false claims could constitute offences under Section 505 of the Penal Code for statements conducing to public mischief and Section 233 of the Communications and Multimedia Act for improper use of network facilities or services.
Last week, Attorney-General Tan Sri Mohd Dusuki Mokhtar said the A-GC had returned the investigation papers to the police for further investigation.
Police have recorded statements from 25 witnesses, but several aspects, including verification of CCTV footage, require further examination before the probe can be completed.
fd45063e34584fb5: JERUSALEM: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu called on Sunday for an investigation into the anonymous sources featured in the award-winning Gaza war documentary "NAZA."
The film is based on testimony from 24 unnamed Israeli military whistleblowers who accuse the army of killing numerous civilians in Gaza with the use of AI-powered targeting systems.

"Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu this evening asked the chief of staff of the Israeli army, the head of the Shin Bet (domestic intelligence), and the state attorney to open a thorough investigation targeting the participants in the film 'NAZA' and to prosecute them," Netanyahu's office said in a statement.
"NAZA" takes its name from the Israeli military term for civilian casualties expected in airstrikes, an abbreviated form of the Hebrew phrase for "collateral damage."
Awarded a special jury prize at the Venice Film Festival, the film received a historic 25-minute standing ovation, but it has triggered a political storm in Israel.
"This film tells a false, misleading and biased story that defames the State of Israel and the army around the world," Netanyahu said, according to the statement.
He has previously declared his intention to back legislation to strip citizenship from people who "defame" soldiers.
The Israeli army, for its part, has "categorically" rejected the accusations contained in the film, expressing doubts about the reliability of the anonymous contributors.

Launched in retaliation for Hamas's deadly Oct 7, 2023 attacks, Israel's military campaign in Gaza has killed more than 74,000 people, according to the territory's health ministry, which operates under Hamas authority and whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations.--AFP
14a7dc24e475c845: PUCHONG: A fire in Bandar Bukit Puchong yesterday destroyed two lorries and damaged two factories.
Videos of the blaze, showing thick black smoke billowing over the premises as flames engulfed part of a factory, have since gone viral on social media.
"The operations commander reported that the fire involved two factories," the Selangor Fire and Rescue Department said in a statement issued at 7.10pm.
The premises belonged to Armlink Machinery Removal Sdn Bhd and Skymatics Holdings Sdn Bhd.
The Armlink Machinery Removal factory, measuring 80 by 100 sq ft, was estimated to be 80 per cent damaged, while the 240 by 200 sq ft Skymatics Holdings factory sustained about 30 per cent damage.
"The fire also involved two lorries, which were 100 per cent burnt," the department said.

7ee3e4207077a193: INDORE, India: Abhishek Sharma struck a quick 69 before Arshdeep Singh's three wickets helped India to a 14-run win over the West Indies in the third T20 international on Sunday.
Opener Abhishek's 30-ball assault guided India to 223 all out, a total their bowlers defended by restricting West Indies to 209-7 in Indore, giving them 2-1 lead in the five-match series.
"It was wonderful to see the bowlers being confident," India captain Shreyas Iyer said.
"The clarity was very much visible when I was interacting. They were ready to take up the challenge and that's what we want."
The previous two games had been won by the team batting second, as the West Indies knocked off a target of 250 to level the series on Friday, pulling off the second highest successful chase in T20Is.
Abhishek handed India a quick start as he put on 108 runs with fellow left-hander Ishan Kishan, who made 37, after India were put in to bat.
Sanju Samson fell for just three before India's batters responded with regular boundaries, Abhishek reaching his fifty off 18 balls.
Spinner Roston Chase broke the stand as he removed Kishan and then dismissed Iyer for one in the same over.
Pace bowler Shamar Springer cut short Abhishek's knock, which featured six fours and five sixes, as India began to wobble.
Tilak Varma (28) and Nitish Kumar Reddy (21) kept the score ticking over as wickets continued to fall.
Lower-order contributions from Axar Patel, who hit 20, and Prince Yadav, who made an unbeaten 13 off six balls, boosted the total.
"Probably with the ball, we could've executed a little bit better," said West Indies skipper Shai Hope. "So those little margins would be the deciding factor come the end of the game."

In reply, West Indies Hope, who made an unbeaten 102 in the previous series-levelling win, for five off left-arm quick Arshdeep before Shimron Hetmyer hit the same bowler for a six and three fours in a 19-run over.
Hetmyer made 43 off 26 balls before being dismissed by Naman Dhir and Rovman Powell fell for five as West Indies slipped in their chase.
Dhir struck again to send back opener Kamil Pooran, who hit a 27-ball 42, to reduce the opposition to 105-4 in the 11th over.
Sherfane Rutherford attempted to repeat his heroics for the second game, clubbing 32 off 20 before Arshdeep bowled him in the 18th over to effectively extinguish West Indies' hopes.
The fourth match is on Wednesday in Hyderabad. — AFP

a17b53e97777fa66: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 12 — Air quality deteriorated across several states this morning, with 22 of the country's 68 monitoring stations recording unhealthy Air Pollutant Index (API) levels as schools in multiple states prepared to resume physical classes.
According to Department of Environment (DOE) surveillance data as of 8.46am, only three stations recorded good air quality while 42 were in the moderate range.

Johor emerged as the hardest-hit state, accounting for eight unhealthy stations, including the nation's highest reading of 170 in Kota Tinggi. Elevated figures were also logged in Pasir Gudang (168), Pengerang (164), Larkin (160), Tangkak (156), Batu Pahat (152), Kluang (152), and Segamat (129).
In Negeri Sembilan, Seremban recorded 164, Nilai posted 163, and coastal Port Dickson stood at 137.

Pahang logged three unhealthy stations, comprising Balok Baru in Kuantan at 162, Rompin at 157, and Indera Mahkota in Kuantan at 142. In Terengganu, elevated readings were recorded across Kemaman (157), Paka (156), and Kuala Terengganu (154).
In Melaka, Bukit Rambai logged 153, while Alor Gajah hovered just over the line at 101.
Across the Greater Klang Valley, Putrajaya registered 146, peat fire hotspot Johan Setia in Selangor recorded 129, and Cheras in Kuala Lumpur stood at 123.

The morning spike in pollution comes as schools in Melaka, Negeri Sembilan, Pahang, Putrajaya, alongside parts of Kuala Lumpur and Selangor, were scheduled to resume regular classroom sessions today following decisions made yesterday afternoon based on 2pm moderate readings.

In Melaka, education authorities had greenlit reopenings after recording sub-100 readings yesterday, including Alor Gajah at 91 and Bukit Rambai at 94. However, both areas worsened overnight, with Bukit Rambai climbing back into the unhealthy bracket at 153 this morning.

In Putrajaya, where authorities noted readings had remained consistently below the 150 closure threshold over three days, air quality climbed from 70 yesterday afternoon to 146 this morning, hovering just beneath the closure benchmark.

Conversely, Cheras registered steady improvement, easing from 152 yesterday to 123 today. Schools under the Bangsar/Pudu District Education Office had been ordered closed yesterday due to localized pollution.
In Selangor, schools under the Hulu Langat, Gombak, and Petaling Perdana district education offices were similarly kept shut yesterday.

Health and education authorities have advised parents, high-risk groups, and students exhibiting respiratory symptoms to wear protective face masks and track real-time air quality updates via official channels.

7a0518e82f68d9b2: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 12 — Child advocacy group Protect & Save The Children Malaysia (PS the Children) has welcomed the child safety measures in Budget 2027, but urged the government to establish dedicated, transparent funding to guarantee their execution.

The group commended the explicit recognition of online child sexual exploitation in the national budget speech, noting that the screen in a child's hands has become a primary staging ground for abuse.

Key budget pledges include upgrading the police D11 division’s Malaysia Internet Crime Against Children (MICAC) system with advanced analytics, expanding the Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission’s school safety campaigns, enforcing the Online Safety Act, and training 6,000 caregivers under a RM100 million matching grant.

To highlight the urgency, the group cited police statistics of 892 child sexual crime cases between January and October 2025 alone, while an inter-agency study estimated that roughly 100,000 Malaysian adolescents aged 12 to 17 experience online sexual exploitation annually, with half suffering in total silence.
Executive director Amnani Abdul Kadir warned that digital enforcement tools represent only one part of the solution.

"But technology alone cannot protect a child who does not know that what is happening to her is abuse," she said, insisting that school prevention, accessible reporting channels, and survivor recovery must receive equal funding priority.

The group also urged Putrajaya to publish dedicated child protection line items in the budget, mandate digital safety curricula in schools, enforce platform accountability, and strengthen mandatory background screening for all individuals working with children.
ed2a6ba6ec2af189: OCTOBER 12 — When President Donald Trump learnt that the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize had gone to Navanethem “Navi” Pillay rather than himself, he expressed his disappointment. He dismissed her as a “mystery person”, saying he had never heard of her.
Pillay’s reaction to the news was one of disbelief. She reportedly asked, “Is it April Fool’s Day?”

The chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee, Jørgen Watne Frydnes, had initially been unable to reach her by telephone. He later told the BBC that he had been trying to contact her to deliver the news.

Frydnes said Pillay’s work had been “instrumental in ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide are prosecuted”. He described her commitment to universal legal principles and her firm moral compass as constants throughout her long career.
At a time of escalating wars and conflicts, Frydnes stressed, international law was no longer merely a supplement to peace and security, but “an absolute necessity”.

Pillay’s recognition comes at a time when international justice institutions face mounting pressure. Her career is a reminder that defending the rule of law requires courage, particularly when accountability challenges the powerful.

Born in Durban in 1941 to a family of Indian Tamil origin, Pillay grew up under apartheid. Her father, Narrainsamy Naidoo, worked as a bus driver and took on other jobs to support his eight children, determined to provide them with a good education despite the constraints of the time.

Growing up in a society where race restricted opportunity, Pillay went on to challenge the very system that had shaped her early life. In 1967, she established her own legal practice, defending those who faced discrimination under apartheid. It was the beginning of a career devoted to justice, human rights and holding power accountable.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Growing up in a society where race restricted opportunity, Navi Pillay went on to challenge the very system that had shaped her early life. — AFP pic

Her career subsequently took her to the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, where she served as a judge and president, and later to the International Criminal Court. She went on to become the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, championing the rights of the vulnerable and confronting abuses of power.

As chair of the UN Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including East Jerusalem, and Israel, Pillay oversaw a report published in September 2025 that concluded Israel was responsible for genocide in Gaza, a finding Israel rejected.
She dedicated her Nobel award to survivors of international crimes, reflecting her longstanding commitment to justice for victims.

But recognition takes many forms. Some people receive international honours for their contributions. Others are recognised only after years of injustice, while some leave behind achievements that continue to shape the world long after their names have faded from public memory.

Among Nobel laureates of Indian origin are Rabindranath Tagore, awarded the Literature Prize in 1913 for Gitanjali; physicist C. V. Raman, who won the Physics Prize in 1930 for the Raman Effect; Mother Teresa, honoured with the Peace Prize in 1979; economist Amartya Sen, awarded the economics prize in 1998; and Kailash Satyarthi, who shared the 2014 Nobel Peace Prize for his work against child labour and for children’s rights.
Beyond these celebrated names are extraordinary Indian minds whose contributions have shaped science, industry and human knowledge, without always receiving the recognition they deserve.

Nambi Narayanan, the aerospace scientist whose work advanced India’s rocket propulsion programme, was arrested in 1994 in connection with an espionage case involving allegations that sensitive space programme secrets had been sold to foreign countries. The allegations against him were later found to be baseless.
After years of legal battles and personal hardship, his name was cleared, and in 2018 the Supreme Court directed the Kerala government to pay him compensation.

Narayanan’s story is a sobering reminder that recognition can be delayed not merely by neglect, but by injustice. The value of his work did not change during the years in which his reputation was under a cloud. What changed was the world’s understanding of what had happened to him.

Then there is G. D. Naidu, the self-taught inventor from Coimbatore often called the “Edison of India”. His interests spanned engineering, transport, agriculture and practical technical education. He built machines, developed inventions and established a transport enterprise, driven by an instinct for solving everyday problems through technology.
Naidu received the Padma Bhushan in 1970. Yet his story raises another question: how many people today know the extent of his work?

Further back in history stands Brahmagupta, the mathematician who lived from 598 to 668 CE. He did not invent zero from nothing, but made a crucial contribution by setting out rules for arithmetic involving zero and negative numbers in his work Brahmasphutasiddhanta, written in 628 CE.

Today, zero is indispensable to mathematics, science, computing and everyday life. We use it constantly without necessarily remembering the scholars who helped establish the mathematical principles that made its use possible. Brahmagupta’s contribution has become part of humanity’s intellectual inheritance, even when the person behind it is unfamiliar to many.

Their stories remind us that recognition is not always timely, fair or lasting. Pillay’s career has earned international acclaim; Narayanan had to fight to clear his name; Naidu’s achievements risk fading from public memory; and Brahmagupta’s contribution lives on in mathematics, even when the man himself is hardly remembered.

Beyond them are millions of others whose work has improved lives, advanced knowledge and strengthened communities. Not every contribution receives an award, makes headlines or finds its way into history books. That does not make it any less valuable.

Trump wanted the world to recognise him. Pillay’s work speaks for itself. And beyond them are countless people whose contributions have changed the world without their names ever becoming household words.
Recognition may bring a name into the headlines. It is what we leave behind that gives it meaning.

f630a4f4383fd298: KUALA LUMPUR: IKEA Malaysia is evolving its retail approach as changing consumer behaviour and digital shopping reshape how Malaysians shop for home furnishings.
The Swedish home furnishing retailer is strengthening its omnichannel model, combining physical stores, online shopping, home delivery and collection points.
IKEA Malaysia Country Retail Director Takeshi Murai said the upcoming Kuching store would reflect this approach.
The smaller format is designed around inspiration and product experiences as part of a wider shopping journey.
"We want the physical meeting point stores to be a source of inspiration, to be a source of touch and feel," he told Business Times.
BEYOND THE LARGE-FORMAT STORE
The shift does not mean IKEA is moving away from physical retail, but broadening how customers access its products and services.
Murai said IKEA wanted to get "closer and closer" to consumers, but this did not necessarily mean opening a traditional large-format store in every location.
He said the immediate focus was on making the Kuching store successful while the company explored other ways to improve accessibility.
In Ipoh, consumers can order IKEA products and have them delivered to an IKEA collection point.
The company is also developing services such as online interior design to expand digital channels in its retail ecosystem.
"We are trying not only to bring IKEA stores, which can sometimes take time, but also to bring IKEA closer to customers in other ways," said Murai.
IKEA's retail and product strategy is also being shaped by changes in how Malaysians live.
Murai said the company regularly visits homes and speaks to consumers about their needs and aspirations.
One major challenge identified was storage and organisation, particularly as more Malaysians live in smaller urban homes and apartments.
"So we are trying to support customers by providing solutions that fit into smaller spaces than in the past," he said.
Murai added that IKEA could draw on its global experience in small-space living, particularly from markets such as Tokyo, to develop solutions for Malaysian consumers.
KUCHING INTRODUCES NEW RETAIL FORMAT
IKEA Kuching, scheduled to open in December, will be the retailer's first store in East Malaysia.
IKEA Kuching will be smaller than IKEA Malaysia's existing large-format stores, reflecting efforts to develop different store formats for different markets.
Murai said IKEA was continuously exploring new ways of meeting customers, with its stores around the world differing in size and layout.
He said the Kuching format was being developed around the idea that physical stores should complement, rather than compete with, digital shopping.
"The concept brings together the physical store, online shopping, home delivery and collection points to provide customers with greater flexibility."
The new store is also expected to deepen IKEA's presence in East Malaysia while creating local employment opportunities.
The majority of employees are being recruited in Sarawak, while some employees from Peninsular Malaysia have been brought in to provide operational experience and training.
"Our ambition is to develop the Kuching store together with Sarawak and the people of Kuching. That is why about 90 per cent of our recruitment is coming from local people in Sarawak," Murai said.
AFFORDABILITY REMAINS KEY
Affordability is still a major priority as consumers navigate changing household budgets.
Murai said IKEA had recently lowered the prices of multiple products.
More than 1,200 products are now priced below RM10, while more than 300 are priced below RM5.
He added that the retailer's integrated supply chain, from product design to logistics, helped it manage costs.
"When we design our new range, we introduce more than 1,000 new products. At the same time, we design the price together with the product."
Murai said global purchasing volumes also allowed IKEA to secure lower costs, supporting its low-price proposition.
He said affordability was not about sacrificing quality, design or sustainability, but delivering value for money.
"One of the advantages we have is that, by setting the volumes across all the countries and the world, we can secure lower costs. That is how we achieve low prices for customers.
"It's not only about the price. It's also about quality, design and sustainability."
POSITIVE ON IKEA MALAYSIA'S GROWTH
Looking ahead, Murai said he remained positive about IKEA's prospects in Malaysia as the retailer continued to make its products more affordable, accessible and sustainable.

While he stopped short of giving a specific forecast for the wider retail market, he said IKEA had continued to find better solutions during challenging periods. "I have been through different times at IKEA, and every time things become more challenging, we find better solutions.
"I am looking forward to how we can develop our retail business to be closer to more people, to be more affordable for more people and to be more sustainable.
"I am very positive about it."
For Murai, IKEA's longer-term measure of success goes beyond store numbers or sales.
"Our goal is to create a better life for many Malaysians.
"If we can deliver one piece of IKEA product to every home in Malaysia, maybe I would call it a success," he added.

bc4e3a4072c4392b: DURBAN, South Africa: Steve Smith broke the Test record for the most career catches by a fielder as Australia played themselves into a strong position on the third day of the first Test against South Africa at Kingsmead on Sunday.
Smith held four catches, taking his total to 223, as South Africa were bowled out for 284 in reply to Australia's first innings of 390.
Nic Maddinson (17 not out) and Travis Head (10 not out) added 33 runs off just 5.4 overs to stretch Australia's overall lead to 139 before bad light ended play for the third day in a row.
Maddinson, who laboured to a 33-ball duck in the first innings, hit two fours off Marco Jansen in the first over of the second innings and added a six off Wiaan Mulder before play was called off.
Australia's bowlers applied relentless pressure on an easy-paced pitch and a succession of South African batsmen contributed to their own dismissals by playing poor shots.
Six Protea batters reached 30 but David Bedingham's 49 was the top score.

Australian captain Pat Cummins took three for 54 and Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon claimed two wickets each as Australia's long-serving bowling quartet combined with customary efficiency.
South African batting coach Ashwell Prince defended the approach of his batsmen.
"If you look at the make-up of their bowling attack, they're heavily dependent on the three seamers and Lyon is phenomenal as a spinner able to hold one end up," said Prince.
"But they're going to come with a certain intensity that can only last for a certain period of time. I think that's the learning. Sometimes you've got to be able to absorb that intensity."

Prince said he backed his batsmen to play their own game, even though all of the top three were out caught in the slips trying to play forcing shots, while South Africa captain Temba Bavuma and Kyle Verreynne were caught by Smith at slip when they played reverse sweeps.

"Every player who walks out for every team naturally has their personal approach to batting. Some guys are more aggressive than others. Over long periods of time, they reap the rewards of that and sometimes it doesn't pay off."
Lyon hails Renshaw
Lyon said he expected spin to play a significant role in the remaining two days.
"I felt like (South African spinners) Kesh (Maharaj) and Simon (Harmer) both were spinning out of the middle of the wicket yesterday and I felt the same," said Lyon.

"I did notice when the ball went quite soft that the spin probably dropped down a little bit, but it was a nice breeze out there for me today, so I felt like my shape was pretty good and was pretty happy with it."
Lyon praised Matt Renshaw, who scored 190 and was the senior partner in a record 134-run ninth wicket partnership with Lyon on Saturday that swung the match in Australia's favour.
"He had a very clear plan on how to go about it. I thought Matt Renshaw was absolutely incredible. Not even talking about his knock. just his guidance, his support, the confidence that he instilled."
Smith started the day on 219 catches, one behind Joe Root of England.
He equalled the record when he caught Bavuma. Smith, playing in his 126th Test, broke the record when he lunged to his left from second slip to hold a sharp edge from Bedingham off Cummins.

Smith was in the action again with a spectacular catch to dismiss Verreynne, again anticipating well at slip as the South African wicketkeeper made good contact with a reverse sweep which Smith held in an outstretched right hand.
His fourth catch was from an edge to slip by last man Anrich Nortje off the bowling of Beau Webster.
Smith's career haul of 223 catches exceeds the total of all but 11 specialist wicketkeepers. — AFP

619c2c1b5e547a6f: CHICAGO: Amos Kipruto of Kenya dominated a world-class field to finally win his first Chicago Marathon while Ethiopia's Hawi Feysa defended her women's title on Sunday.
Kipruto's time of 2:01:09 was a new personal best and vindication for the 34-year-old, who had finished second in Chicago last year and third the previous edition.
This time, Kipruto pulled clear of defending champion and pre-race favorite Jacob Kiplimo at mile 21 and never looked back.
"Today's race was really good for me... I came here 2024, I became position three, 2025 I became position two. And now 2026 it was either win or die for me," said Kipruto.

He finished the 48th Chicago Marathon nearly two minutes clear in ideal sunny but cool conditions, briefly sinking to the floor after he crossed the finish line, before quickly rising with a giant grin.
Kipruto, the 2022 London champion, had set his previous personal best finishing fourth at this year's historic London race, where the mythical two-hour barrier was broken.
But he had the spotlight to himself in Chicago.
"The preparation for me toward the Chicago Marathon 2026 was perfect for me. I improved a lot in training for the previous London Marathon," said Kipruto.
"But I said 'let's go (for) Chicago' and let be what will be. Everything is all about a mindset. It was a tough field, but I set my mind and I said 'let's go.'"
His time makes him the joint-fifth fastest marathon runner of all time.
Uganda's Kiplimo ultimately slipped back to fourth place.
Tadese Takele Bikila of Ethiopia – the defending Tokyo champion, making his US marathon debut – took second, while compatriot Milkesa Mengesha came third.
'Elated'
On the women's side, defending champion Feysa also set a new personal best with a blistering 2:13:33.
"I'm elated to have won the second time," said Feysa, via an interpreter.
She was followed by Sharon Lokedi of Kenya, this year's Boston winner, who stayed with Feysa most of the race but finished 34 seconds back.

ef92c13804911123: KUALA LUMPUR: When someone undergoes coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery, attention naturally centres on the heart. Yet the operation can also leave patients with a sizeable wound on the leg, where a vein is often taken to create the bypass.
Traditionally, removing that vein involves a long incision along the leg. Endoscopic vein harvesting (EVH) offers a less invasive alternative, using a small opening and a camera to guide the removal.

Consultant cardiothoracic surgeon Dr Zamrin Dimon said the technique can result in smaller scars, less pain, faster wound healing and a lower risk of complications, particularly for patients who may already have difficulty healing, such as those with diabetes.
CABG is recommended when several major coronary arteries are significantly narrowed or blocked, with the aim of improving blood flow to the heart.

“What we do is create a new vessel or conduit taken from another part of the body, such as the artery from the chest, the radial artery from the arm, or the saphenous vein from the leg," Zamrin explained.

The saphenous vein is commonly used because it is relatively long, large and lies close beneath the skin. Patients who need multiple bypasses may require more than one graft, with a single vein segment measuring around 18-20cm.
Under the conventional approach, known as open vein harvesting, removing that amount of vein can mean a wound almost as long as the vein itself.
“If we need 40cm of vein, the wound on the leg can be 40cm long. So, imagine having a large scar on your chest and then having another long scar on your leg," Zamrin said.
The issue is not only cosmetic: a large leg wound can become an added burden during recovery, especially if it heals slowly.
“Sometimes after five or six weeks, the wound is still open and wet, and patients will need frequent dressing - especially diabetic patients,” he added.
Pain and discomfort can also make patients less willing to move around soon after surgery, even though early mobilisation is important in reducing the risk of blood clots and other complications.

With EVH, the surgeon instead makes a small opening and inserts an endoscope, or tiny camera, to guide the removal of the vein from inside the leg. Most of the surrounding skin remains intact, leaving only a few small incisions, each around 4cm.
That difference can make recovery easier. Zamrin said the smaller wounds may heal within two to three days, allowing patients to start moving sooner and return more comfortably to daily activities.

EVH is not necessarily quicker, however. The technique can take about an hour or slightly longer, compared with around 45 minutes for conventional harvesting, particularly when a longer segment of vein is needed.
It also requires specialised training and surgical experience, which is one reason it is not yet used for every bypass operation.
Zamrin stressed that EVH is not intended to replace conventional vein harvesting in all cases; rather, it gives suitable patients another option to discuss with their surgeon.
Most patients can be considered for the technique, although those with varicose veins, very superficial veins or veins that are too thin may not be suitable.

bf6e49404cb9430f: VAUGHN Taylor birdied the second playoff hole to defeat Germany's Alex Cejka and win his first PGA Tour Champions title at the Constellation Furyk & Friends on Sunday in Palm Coast, Fla.

After the players parred the par-4 18th on the first playoff hole, they replayed the hole at the Ocean Course at Hammock Beach. Taylor stuck his approach shot about 6 feet from the cup and rolled in the ensuing birdie putt with ease.
Taylor, in his first season on tour after turning 50 in March, had three top-10 finishes across August and September but never better than a T7 before his breakthrough this weekend.

"I was just trying to, you know, tell myself to hang in there," Taylor said. "You know, don't give up; stay strong. You know, trying to calm my nerves. But I just wanted to finish strong and not give it away or do something stupid and lousy. Just kept fighting, trying to keep my emotions in check."
Taylor began the day three shots behind leader Mathew Goggin of Australia. He rolled in five straight birdies at Nos. 10-14 on his way to a 4-under-par 68 to tie Cejka at 17-under 199.

"That's the biggest thing in golf, is just momentum," Taylor said. "I mean, momentum is everything in this game. It can help you and hurt you, and just if you get a couple in a row or just get things going in a positive direction it can completely flip your pessimistic mind and it can turn that off."
Cejka had shot his second straight round of 65 and finished his bogey-free day by birdieing No. 18 to take the clubhouse lead at 17 under.

He and Taylor had to wait and watch Australian Michael Wright, who took the outright lead at 18 under after birdieing Nos. 15 and 16. Wright needed par at the last hole to win in regulation, but he needed to take a drop after two poor shots.

He failed to save bogey, which would have put him in the playoff at 17 under, and carded a double-bogey 6 instead. Wright (69) finished alone in third at 16 under. Ben Crane (65), Argentina's Angel Cabrera (67), Ryan Armour (69), Australia's Rod Pampling (72) and Goggin (73) tied for fourth at 15 under.
Cejka said he wasn't envisioning a playoff when he stepped off the 18th green, as Wright was still ahead.

"You are always disappointed if you lose in a playoff. (But) today was a great day. Gave me a lot of chances," Cejka said. "I started like, I don't know, eighth, 10th position, so to make it all the way to the playoff, I'm very satisfied. To lose against a birdie, there is nothing you can do."

Taylor is projected to rise 16 spots to No. 21 in the Charles Schwab Cup points race with one tournament left in the regular season. Following next week's SAS Championship, the top 72 players will advance to the first leg of the three-week Schwab Cup playoffs.

Goggin, who had to play his way into the field via qualifying on Tuesday, may have come up short of winning but will get a valuable boost to No. 74 in the points race, giving him a chance to make the playoffs. — REUTERS

5107dd38ad25f0b1: KUALA LUMPUR: The UM Mastery in Innovative Teaching (UM MINT) Colloquium and the International University Carnival on E-Learning (IUCEL) 2026 brought together 216 participants from 26 institutions to exchange ideas and innovative teaching practices.

Hosted by Universiti Malaya (UM) at Wyndham Grand Bangsar here on Thursday and Friday, the two-day programme brought together academic staff, researchers, instructional designers, educational technologists, e-learning practitioners and policymakers.

UM deputy vice-chancellor (Academic and International) Professor Dr Hasniza Zaman Huri said higher education is changing rapidly with the rise of artificial intelligence (AI) and digital technologies.
This made continuous innovation in teaching methods, assessment, student engagement and learning design increasingly important, she said.
"We need to rethink not only what we teach, but how we teach and how students learn."
Hasniza added that AI is a key focus of the event, but the challenge is balancing its use with students' ability to think independently.
"AI is our main agenda nowadays. But how do we balance AI and the cognitive thinking process in our students? I think that is the main issue we are discussing.

"We want to encourage the use of AI to enhance teaching and learning, but at the same time, we do not want our students to surrender their cognitive thinking process. That is the key point we are addressing."
She said educators could not avoid the technology and had to ensure it was used responsibly.
"We cannot run from AI. AI is, of course, embedded, but how do we govern its use responsibly? That is our key point here."
Hasniza said UM has an AI policy for teaching and learning. Students and lecturers could use AI, but they had to declare its use.
Sessions on AI and the future of teaching also explored how educators could move beyond content delivery to develop human capabilities.
The programme also featured human-centred e-learning and cybergogy, which Hasniza said went beyond using technology for its own sake.
Instead, it focused on supporting active, collaborative and personalised learning.
She added that technology had to keep the younger generation engaged.

"Our technology should be able to enhance teaching and learning, especially for the new generation. We have to come up with something innovative and creative so that our students will be more attentive in class and more excited to attend lessons," she said.
UM MINT, themed "The Future of Teaching Mastery", focused on teaching excellence, reflective practice and the sharing of innovative approaches.

It included the Spark & Share Rapid Talks Colloquium, where educators presented practical approaches involving digital tools, innovative assessment strategies, evidence-based practices and lessons from classroom implementation.
Meanwhile, IUCEL 2026, themed "Redefining Cybergogy Beyond Algorithms", highlighted transformative e-learning, digital innovation and human-centred approaches to education.

IUCEL is an annual conference, with Universiti Malaya co-hosting the 2026 edition in collaboration with the Majlis Ketua-Ketua e-Pembelajaran IPTA Malaysia and the Higher Education Ministry . A key component was the Invention, Innovation and Design on E-Learning (IIDEL) Competition. Participants showcased original technology-enhanced learning innovations supporting inclusive, accessible, collaborative and sustainable digital education.
Hasniza said five main awards were presented. Two went to UM, while Universiti Malaysia Sabah, Taylor's University and Universiti Malaysia Perlis each received one.
The programme included keynote and plenary sessions, workshops, educational technology exhibitions, professional networking opportunities and the IUCEL Awards Ceremony.
Hasniza said the event strengthened connections among educators and gave them opportunities to explore new ideas and identify areas for collaboration.
It also encouraged them to translate those ideas into meaningful changes at their respective institutions.
Hasniza added that UM used new technologies showcased at the event to support its teaching and learning.
She said UM MINT would continue to provide a platform for academics to share, exchange and learn from innovative teaching and learning practices.
"Our aim is to build a continuing community of educators who reflect on their practice, experiment with new approaches and collectively shape the future of teaching and learning in higher education.
"UM MINT is more than a teaching colloquium. It is a UM platform to encourage educators to reflect, innovate and rethink how we teach in a rapidly changing world."
Hasniza said the event, together with IUCEL, brought teaching innovation and human-centred digital learning into one conversation.

8bc15d662d20143e: A company announces a major transformation. The chief executive officer uses sophisticated but polished language and tells employees that the organisation will become more digital, agile and customer-focussed.
The employees applaud. Six months later, little has changed. Perhaps the employees understood the announcement but did not understand what it meant for their work.
The above shows why a strategy can be sound on paper but fail if people don't understand what it means for their work.
It underscores the importance of strategic communication and why it is becoming an important leadership competency needed to bring decisions into fruition.
Communication in an organisation no longer means simply transmitting information; it also means providing context to employees.

While in ordinary communication, it may be enough to say "We are restructuring our organisation, strategic communication needs to explain why we are restructuring, what problem we trying to resolve, what it means for employees and where we are going".
Employees today don't just need information; they need context and meaning.
A leader must connect strategy, purpose and action. It is therefore even more important for the leader to explain why.

In an environment that is in a constant state of flux with AI, digitalisation, restructuring, new markets and changing customer expectations, if employees are to be committed to change, it is important that they are told why the change is necessary.
Telling people what to do creates compliance. Explaining why it matters can create commitment.
Nokia provides an example of what can happen when an organisation recognises the need for change but struggles to translate that recognition into timely organisational action.
By the time Nokia responded decisively to the rapid shift towards smartphones, competitors such as Apple and Google had already established strong positions in the market.
The lesson is that recognising change is not enough. Leaders must communicate the urgency of change clearly and ensure that the message is understood and acted upon throughout the organisation.
Some organisations may not choose to communicate everything hoping to inform employees at the right time.
At a time when information travels at lightning speed, it may not be a good idea to withhold information as it would invariably find its way into the hands of the employees.
When explanations from leaders are not forthcoming, employees simply don't stop thinking but they speculate.
If there is a restructuring on the horizon, all sorts of thoughts would come into the minds such as "Is my job safe, Is the company in trouble, what happens next".
The effect can be demoralising for staff, as when leaders leave an information vacuum, employees may fill it with their own interpretations.
Microsoft provides a useful example.
When Satya Nadella became CEO, he sought to shift the company towards a "growth mindset" and greater collaboration.
The change was not simply about introducing new products; employees had to understand a different way of working and thinking.
By communicating the purpose behind the transformation, leadership could connect the company's strategy with what it expected from employees.
Strategic communication is about two-way communication. It is not only communication that flows downwards but also information that flows upwards from employees to decision makers and leaders.
Frontline employees would know what customers are complaining about, where systems are not working, why employees are resisting change and where the strategy is difficult to implement.
Unless there is a two-way flow of communication, an organisation cannot be agile enough to meet the changing expectations of customers.
It is customary for companies to hire communication professionals, but they still cannot replace messages from leaders.
Communication professionals can help formulate messages, but when there is a strategic change, employees expect communication from leaders.
Communication cannot be outsourced when it comes to key issues within the company because these issues require the voice and presence of the leader.
Leadership was once associated with making decisions, setting targets and giving directions.

In an increasingly complex world, decisions would have to be made by different levels of employees, and leaders must explain clearly the thinking behind the decision and elicit feedback from employees who have their hands on the pulse of the customers and the markets.
The leaders of the future must not only know where the organisation is going but also why it is going there.

5d9d09d45176bbb6: SINGAPORE: Seven-time world champion Lewis Hamilton admitted he botched a call over tyres that cost him and Ferrari a second podium place at the Singapore Grand Prix on Sunday.

"He missed the pit entry, and honestly it's a bit of a shame because he's losing a podium also.
